terms.def: The part of a radio that picks out a radio signal and turns it into sound or data you can use.
terms.more: Two key qualities are sensitivity (detecting weak signals) and selectivity (separating signals that are close together).

terms.def: The ability of a receiver to detect the presence of a signal.
terms.more: A more sensitive receiver hears weaker signals. Do not confuse it with selectivity, which is separating one signal from others.

terms.def: The ability of a receiver to discriminate between multiple signals.
terms.more: It lets the receiver pick out the wanted signal from others close by in frequency. Do not confuse it with sensitivity, which is detecting weak signals.

terms.def: The part of a radio that generates the radio signal that is sent to the antenna.
terms.more: Combined with a receiver in one unit it is called a transceiver.

terms.def: A device that combines a receiver and a transmitter.
terms.more: Do not confuse it with a transverter, which converts a transceiver's signals to another band.

terms.def: A circuit used to convert a signal from one frequency to another.
terms.more: It combines two signals and produces new signals at the sum and the difference of their frequencies.

terms.def: A circuit that generates a signal at a specific frequency.
terms.more: A VFO is an oscillator whose frequency you can change.

terms.def: Variable frequency oscillator: the tunable circuit in a transceiver that sets the receive and transmit frequency.
terms.more: Turning the tuning knob adjusts it.

terms.def: A device that converts the RF input and output of a transceiver to another band.
terms.more: It lets a radio be used on a band it does not cover itself. Do not confuse it with a transceiver.

terms.def: A range of frequencies set aside for a particular use, such as the amateur 2-meter band.
terms.more: A transverter moves a transceiver's signals to another band. A strong station on a nearby band, such as FM broadcast near 2 meters, can interfere with a receiver.

terms.def: Push-to-talk: the control that switches a transceiver from receive to transmit.
terms.more: The PTT input switches the transceiver from receive to transmit when it is grounded.

terms.def: Combining speech or other information with an RF carrier signal.
terms.more: It is done by varying the carrier's amplitude, frequency or phase.

terms.def: A plain, steady radio signal that carries no information until it is modulated.
terms.more: Combining speech with an RF carrier is called modulation.

terms.def: A device added to the output of a transceiver to increase the transmitted output power.
terms.more: Some VHF power amplifiers have an SSB or CW-FM switch, which sets the amplifier for proper operation in the selected mode.

terms.def: Single sideband: a voice mode in which the strength of the signal varies with your voice.
terms.more: An amplifier must be set for the mode in use, so some VHF power amplifiers have a switch for SSB or CW-FM.

terms.def: Continuous wave: sending Morse code by switching a radio signal on and off.
terms.more: Some VHF power amplifiers have a switch for SSB or CW-FM that sets the amplifier for proper operation in the selected mode.

terms.def: Frequency modulation: a way of sending voice by varying the frequency of the radio signal.
terms.more: Louder audio makes an FM signal swing farther in frequency. That swing is called deviation.

terms.def: How far an FM signal swings in frequency as you speak.
terms.more: Speaking too loudly or too close to the microphone causes over-deviation and distorted audio. The cure is to talk farther away from the microphone.

terms.def: Unwanted radio energy that disturbs the reception of a radio, TV or other device.
terms.more: Fundamental overload, harmonics and spurious emissions can all cause it.

terms.def: Interference that happens when a receiver is unable to reject a strong signal from outside the band it is tuned to.
terms.more: The weakness is in the receiver, not the transmitter. It is why a broadcast AM or FM radio may pick up an amateur transmission. The cure is a filter at the affected receiver.

terms.def: Unwanted signals at whole-number multiples of the frequency a transmitter is meant to be on.
terms.more: They are one possible cause of radio frequency interference.

terms.def: Unwanted signals that a transmitter puts out on frequencies outside its intended transmission.
terms.more: They are one possible cause of radio frequency interference.

terms.def: Built with transistors and other semiconductor parts instead of vacuum tubes.
terms.more: Most solid-state transmitters reduce output power when SWR is high, to protect the RF output amplifier transistors.

terms.def: Standing wave ratio: a measure of how well the impedance of the antenna matches the feed line.
terms.more: 1:1 is a perfect match. A higher reading such as 4:1 means an impedance mismatch. High SWR can make a solid-state transceiver reduce its output power.

terms.def: A circuit that lets some frequencies pass and blocks others.
terms.more: A filter at the antenna input of an affected receiver can block an amateur signal that is causing interference.

terms.def: A filter that blocks one range of frequencies and lets the rest pass.
terms.more: Installing one can reduce interference to a 2-meter transceiver from a nearby commercial FM station.

terms.def: Interference that seriously disturbs or repeatedly interrupts radio communication.
terms.more: If a neighbor's device causes it to your station: work with the neighbor to find the device, politely explain that FCC rules prohibit it, and check your own station.

terms.def: Federal Communications Commission: the United States government agency that makes and enforces the rules for radio.
terms.more: FCC rules prohibit the use of devices that cause harmful interference.

terms.def: Setting up and operating a station carefully and correctly, the way a responsible amateur is expected to.
terms.more: When interference is reported, first make sure your own station is working properly and meets these standards.

terms.def: A feed line made of a center conductor surrounded by insulation, an outer metal shield and a protective jacket.
terms.more: Moisture contamination causes coax to fail. The jacket should resist ultraviolet light, which can damage it and let water in.

terms.def: The fitting on the end of a coaxial cable that joins it to equipment or to another cable.
terms.more: The first step in resolving interference to coaxial cable TV is to be sure all TV feed line coaxial connectors are installed properly.

terms.def: A station that receives a signal and retransmits it at the same time, so that stations can reach farther.
terms.more: Distorted or unintelligible audio through an FM repeater can come from being slightly off frequency, speaking too loudly or too close to the microphone, or a bad location.

terms.def: Transmitting or receiving a little above or below the frequency you are supposed to be on.
terms.more: A transmitter that is slightly off frequency can sound distorted or unintelligible through an FM repeater.

terms.def: A piece of ferrite material placed around a cable to block unwanted RF from travelling along it.
terms.more: A clip-on ferrite choke on the microphone cable can cure distorted voice transmissions by keeping the transmitted signal from feeding back into the transmitter.

terms.def: A device connected to a transmitter in place of an antenna that turns the transmitter's power into heat.
terms.more: Its primary purpose is to prevent transmitting signals over the air when making tests. A typical one is a 50-ohm non-inductive resistor mounted on a heat sink.

terms.def: A piece of metal that carries heat away from an electronic part so that the part does not overheat.
terms.more: The resistor in an RF dummy load is mounted on one.

terms.def: The unit of resistance and of impedance.
terms.more: A typical RF dummy load is a 50-ohm resistor. Resistance in ohms is measured with an ohmmeter.

terms.def: An instrument that shows how an antenna behaves at different frequencies, including its SWR.
terms.more: It is used to determine if an antenna is resonant at the desired operating frequency.

terms.def: Describes an antenna that is tuned to the frequency in use, so that its feed point acts like a pure resistance.
terms.more: An antenna analyzer is used to find out whether an antenna is resonant at the desired operating frequency.

terms.def: The part of a station that turns the transmitter's RF power into radio waves and picks up radio waves for the receiver.
terms.more: A dummy load takes its place for tests. An SWR of 1:1 means a perfect impedance match between the antenna and the feed line.

terms.def: An instrument that shows how well the impedance of the antenna matches the feed line.
terms.more: A reading of 1:1 indicates a perfect impedance match. A reading of 4:1 indicates an impedance mismatch.

terms.def: The condition where two connected things, such as an antenna and its feed line, have the same impedance, so power passes between them without being reflected.
terms.more: An SWR of 1:1 shows a perfect match. A higher reading such as 4:1 shows a mismatch.

terms.def: The cable that carries radio signals between a radio and its antenna.
terms.more: Power lost in a feed line is converted into heat.

terms.def: The part of a signal's power that is used up inside the feed line instead of reaching the other end.
terms.more: The lost power is converted into heat. Foam-dielectric coaxial cable has less loss per foot than solid-dielectric cable.

terms.def: An instrument that measures the RF power travelling toward the antenna and the power reflected back from it.
terms.more: It can be used to determine SWR, which is worked out from the forward and reflected power readings.

terms.def: Water getting inside a cable.
terms.more: It causes failure of coaxial cables. Water can enter through a jacket damaged by ultraviolet light.

terms.def: The outside plastic covering of a coaxial cable, which protects the parts inside.
terms.more: It should be resistant to ultraviolet light, because ultraviolet light can damage the jacket and allow water to enter the cable.

terms.def: The insulation between the center conductor and the shield of a coaxial cable.
terms.more: Foam-dielectric coaxial cable has less loss per foot than solid-dielectric cable.

terms.def: Another name for voltage: the electrical push between two points, measured in volts.
terms.more: It is measured with a voltmeter, connected in parallel with the component.

terms.def: An instrument that measures electric potential, which is voltage.
terms.more: It is connected in parallel with the component to measure the voltage applied to it.

terms.def: The flow of electricity through a circuit, measured in amperes.
terms.more: It is measured with an ammeter, or a multimeter set for current, connected in series with the component.

terms.def: An instrument that measures electric current.
terms.more: It is connected in series, so that the current flows through the meter.

terms.def: Opposition to the flow of electric current, measured in ohms.
terms.more: It is measured with an ohmmeter or a multimeter, and only when the circuit is not powered.

terms.def: An instrument that measures resistance.
terms.more: It works by applying a small current and measuring the resulting voltage. Make sure the circuit is not powered before measuring in-circuit resistance.

terms.def: A test instrument that combines several meters in one, measuring voltage, current and resistance.
terms.more: To measure current it is connected in series. Trying to measure voltage while it is on the resistance setting can damage it.

terms.def: Connecting a meter or part across a component, with one lead on each end, without breaking the circuit.
terms.more: A voltmeter is connected in parallel. This differs from series, used to measure current, where the meter is inserted in the current path.

terms.def: Connecting a meter or part into the path of the current, so that all the current flows through it.
terms.more: A multimeter set to measure current is connected in series. This differs from parallel, used to measure voltage, where the meter goes across the component.

terms.def: Solder with a corrosive acid flux inside it.
terms.more: It should not be used for radio and electronic work. Rosin-core solder is the usual choice for electronics.

terms.def: A poor solder connection in which the solder did not flow and bond properly.
terms.more: A cold tin-lead solder joint has a rough or lumpy surface. A good one looks bright or shiny.

terms.def: A component that stores electrical energy as it charges.
terms.more: An ohmmeter connected across a large, discharged capacitor shows increasing resistance with time, as the capacitor charges.
